nameStory: The 'decorated' part of this spider's name comes from the ornate red and black patterns adorning its tiny body, like nature's own miniature artwork. The 'money spider' nickname comes from an old European folklore belief that if one of these tiny spiders landed on you, it would bring financial good fortune. The scientific name 'ornatus' literally means 'decorated' in Latin, reinforcing just how striking these little arachnids appear under close inspection.
description: The Decorated Red-and-black Money Spider is a tiny member of the sheetweb weaver family, so small you might mistake it for a speck of dirt at first glance. Despite their diminutive size, these spiders pack impressive visual punch with their contrasting red and black markings that make them look like tiny jewels. They're part of a large family of small spiders that build delicate sheet webs rather than the classic orb webs most people picture. Like other money spiders, they're so lightweight they can actually 'balloon' through the air on silk threads.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny spider, easily overlooked and often mistaken for a small beetle or debris until you see it move with typical spider gait

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Distinctive red and black coloration creates a decorated appearance - the contrast is quite striking when viewed with a hand lens or magnifying glass

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds small, flat sheet webs close to the ground that feel delicate and filmy to the touch, often with a slight sheen in morning dew

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen typical of money spiders, with relatively long legs that give it a delicate, almost fragile appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly across its sheet web when disturbed, often dropping to the ground and 'playing dead' when threatened

habitat: Look for these tiny spiders in low vegetation, leaf litter, and grassy areas throughout New England's forests and field edges. They prefer somewhat moist environments where they can build their sheet webs among moss, fallen leaves, or low-growing plants. You're most likely to spot them in mixed hardwood forests or transitional zones between woods and meadows.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build their characteristic sheet webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and actively hunting, their webs becoming more noticeable in morning dew.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced before adults die off with first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as eggs or early instars hidden in leaf litter and protected crevices.

funFact: These spiders are so light they can actually fly! They release silk threads that catch air currents, allowing them to balloon hundreds of miles through the atmosphere - sometimes entire swarms rain down from the sky in a phenomenon called 'gossamer showers.'
confusionNotes: With only 3 recorded observations in New England, this species might be confused with other tiny red and black spiders or even small beetles. The key is watching for typical spider movement patterns and looking for the sheet web nearby - beetles don't build webs!
contextualKnowledge: Money spiders get their common name from old European folklore, but don't expect riches if one lands on you - though finding one of these rare beauties in New England might feel like hitting the jackpot for spider enthusiasts!
compareHints: Since this is the only Tmeticus species recorded in our dataset, compare it to other linyphiid money spiders by looking for the specific red and black 'decorated' pattern. Most other money spiders in New England are brown, tan, or have different color combinations, making the red-black contrast of T. ornatus quite distinctive among its sheetweb weaver relatives.
